macro_segments.title: The Case of Unspecified Mincha of Esronim: Chachamim vs. Rabbi's Positions

micro_segments.title: Introduction to the Mishnah: A vow of mincha with esronim and uncertainty about the amount
Tanu Rabbanan: The detailed Talmudic version of bringing sixty esronim with stipulation
Mathematical calculation: Sum of numbers 1-60 equals 1,830 using the Tosafot method
Rabbi's position: Bringing 1-60 esronim separately, multiplied by 5 types equals 9,150
The core debate: Can one mix obligatory vow with additional free-will offering in one vessel?

macro_segments.title: Rav Chisda's Framework: The Debate Between Permitting and Prohibiting Non-Sanctified Matter in the Azarah

micro_segments.title: Rav Chisda's initial formulation: Can one bring non-sanctified matter into the Azarah?
Rabbi's position: Prohibits bringing non-sanctified matter, hence separate vessels required
Chachamim's position: Permits bringing non-sanctified matter into the Azarah
Rava's correction: Both agree chullin is forbidden; the real debate is mixing obligation with free-will

macro_segments.title: The Problem of Mixed Kometz and Shirayim: Can you take two kematzim from a mixture?

micro_segments.title: Abaye to Rava: If obligation and free-will are mixed, you need two kematzim
The practical problem: Each kematz might contain both obligation and free-will
Solution through attribution to kohen's hand: Designate first kematz as obligation, second as free-will
The concern: If the vow was for sixty, there is no free-will portion, so the second kematz burns remnants incorrectly
Rabbi Eliezer's solution: Treat doubtful second kematz as fuel, not as a ritual offering

macro_segments.title: Rav Acha's Alternative: The Debate Hinges on Rabbi Eliezer's Doctrine, Not on Mixing Per Se

micro_segments.title: Rav Acha's proposal: Maybe everyone agrees mixing is permitted; the debate is whether Rabbi Eliezer's fuel doctrine applies
Objection: This would require Rabbi to reject Rabbi Eliezer; a technical solution alone cannot account for the disagreement
The practical solution: Bring sixty in one vessel and one esaron in a second vessel with mouths touching
How the touching-vessel solution works: Ensure there is always a separate nedava portion to take kematz from

macro_segments.title: Rava's Resolution: The Debate Centers on Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's Oil Proportionality Doctrine

micro_segments.title: Rava's position: Everyone agrees on mixing; the true debate is whether oil must be proportional per esaron or fixed at one log
Mishnah quotation: Chachamim require sixty log for sixty esaron; Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires only one log
The practical implication: If one log is always required, you cannot mix different amounts in one vessel
Chachamim hold proportional oil; Rabbi holds like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's fixed one-log rule

macro_segments.title: Rav Ashi's Alternative: Debate over Whether a Vow Specifies Exact Amount or Minimum Amount

micro_segments.title: Rav Ashi's framework: The debate may turn on whether a vow means an exact amount or a minimum
Chachamim: If you said X, bringing more than X satisfies the vow (minimum interpretation)
Rabbi: If you said X, you must bring exactly X; anything more creates unwanted mixture
Verification: This exact-vs.-minimum debate appears elsewhere in the Talmud regarding animal sacrifices
Why mincha differs from animals: In mincha, the entire amount becomes one kometz regardless of size; in animals, the internal organs differ
Bottom line: Rebbe requires separate vessels because X means exactly X, and mixing obligation with free-will creates multiple problems

macro_segments.title: Mishnah on Voluntary Offerings of Wood, Frankincense, and Metals

micro_segments.title: Mishnah: If you vow to bring wood, the minimum is two logs; if you say wood singular, one log suffices
Frankincense vow: The minimum is a kometz of frankincense, equated to the five kematzim standard amounts
Gold: Minimum vow is one gold dinar; silver is one silver dinar; copper is valued at one silver ma'ah

macro_segments.title: Tanu Rabbanan on Mandatory Altar Offering: Why Frankincense is the Default When Unspecified

micro_segments.title: If you say you vow to the altar without specifying what, you must bring frankincense as the default offering
Minimum for frankincense is a kometz, derived from biblical comparison to the mincha kometz

macro_segments.title: Mishnah on Voluntary Offerings of Wood, Frankincense, and Metals (continued)

micro_segments.title: Uncertainty: If you said you vow to the altar but forgot what, bring from each category of permitted offerings

macro_segments.title: Tanu Rabbanan on Mandatory Altar Offering: Why Frankincense is the Default When Unspecified (continued)

micro_segments.title: Reasoning: Frankincense is the only offering entirely consumed by the altar; other offerings leave portions for the kohanim or other uses
Gemara exceptions: Olah, olat ha-of, nesachim, and minchat nesachim all get wholly or partially burnt, yet are excluded
Reasoning for exclusion: While some offerings are wholly consumed, frankincense is the default mental image of an altar offering

macro_segments.title: Precision in Metal Vows: Coins vs. Ingots, and the Spike-and-Fork Examples

micro_segments.title: Gold vow clarification: When you say gold, you mean a gold coin (dinar), not an ingot or small change
Silver vow clarification: When you say silver, you mean a silver coin (dinar), not ingots or loose change
Silver small change caveat: Only applies in places where silver small change is not commonly used for transactions
Copper vow: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov interprets as a small copper fork or tine used for cleaning lamps
Iron vow: When you say iron, the default is an amount sufficient to make a roof spike to ward off ravens
